---
title: "Getting started with zuxlsx"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zuxlsx)
```

zuxlsx reads `.xlsx` workbooks into R. It needs no system XML, ZIP or
cryptography library: the parts it builds on are compiled into the package, so
installing it is all there is to do. It reads; it does not write -- see the end
of this article for what to use instead.

The examples use a small workbook that comes with the package.

```{r}
path <- system.file("extdata", "two-sheets.xlsx", package = "zuxlsx")
```

## What is in the workbook

`xlsx_sheets()` lists the worksheets, in the order the workbook keeps them.
It reads only the workbook's index, not the sheets, so it costs the same on a
small file as on a large one.

```{r}
xlsx_sheets(path)
```

## Reading a worksheet

`xlsx_read()` reads a worksheet into a data frame. By default it reads the
first worksheet and takes the column names from its first row.

```{r}
readings <- xlsx_read(path)
readings
```

Each column takes the type its cells support. Nothing had to be declared: the
numbers are doubles, the `TRUE`/`FALSE` cells are logical, and the dates --
which an `.xlsx` stores as numbers with a date format -- are `Date`s.

```{r}
vapply(readings, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1))
```

A column that mixes kinds of value, or holds a string or a cell error such as
`#DIV/0!`, becomes character, with each cell as it was written. A date that
carries a time of day becomes `POSIXct` rather than losing the time.

## Choosing a worksheet, and part of one

`sheet` takes a name or a position.

```{r}
xlsx_read(path, sheet = "notes")
identical(xlsx_read(path, sheet = 2), xlsx_read(path, sheet = "notes"))
```

`range` takes a rectangle in A1 notation. Either corner may name a cell, a
column or a row, so `"B1:C3"`, `"A:B"` and `"2:4"` all work.

```{r}
xlsx_read(path, range = "B1:C3")
```

When the first row of what is read is data rather than names, say so with
`col_names = FALSE`, and the columns are named by position.

```{r}
xlsx_read(path, range = "A2:B4", col_names = FALSE)
```

Without `range`, the table is the rectangle the worksheet's non-empty cells
span, so one that starts further down the sheet, at `B3` say, reads with its
header from row 3.

## When something is wrong

Every error zuxlsx raises carries a condition class, and the class -- not the
wording of the message -- is what to rely on. A file that is not there is an
input error; one that is not a ZIP archive at all is a ZIP error; a damaged
part is an XML or ZIP error naming the part.

```{r}
not_a_workbook <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
writeLines("this is not a spreadsheet", not_a_workbook)

tryCatch(
  xlsx_read(not_a_workbook),
  zuxlsx_zip_error = function(e) "not a readable xlsx file",
  zuxlsx_error = function(e) "some other problem"
)
```

Every class is a subclass of `zuxlsx_error`, so one handler can catch them
all. `?"zuxlsx-conditions"` lists them. One is worth knowing early: a
password-protected workbook read without a password is
`zuxlsx_encrypted_error`, and every reader takes `password =` to open one.

## When a data frame is the wrong shape

A worksheet is not always a table: a report with stacked blocks, a header
several rows deep, notes in the margins. For those, `xlsx_cells()` returns one
row per cell, with its position, its own type and its text, and
`xlsx_rows()` returns the sheet row by row as text. `xlsx_stream_cells()` reads
a sheet a chunk at a time, for one too large to hold, or to stop as soon as
something is found.

```{r}
head(xlsx_cells(path))
```

## Writing workbooks

zuxlsx does not write `.xlsx` files, and is not going to. For that, use
[writexl](https://docs.ropensci.org/writexl/) for a plain data frame or
[openxlsx2](https://janmarvin.github.io/openxlsx2/) when formatting matters.
